claims.text: The compared Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni quinary alloy and its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets can be prepared as comparable single-phase FCC microstructures.
All alloy variants should be tensile-tested at room temperature using the same strain rate.
Adding the constituents present in the quinary alloy enhances local chemical ordering relative to its lower-constituent subsets.
The quinary alloy has stronger lattice distortions than the quaternary and ternary alloys.
Differences in local chemical ordering and lattice distortion lower the stacking-fault energy of the quinary alloy relative to the quaternary and ternary subsets.
Lower stacking-fault energy promotes earlier or more extensive deformation twinning.
Dislocation activity combined with deformation-induced nanotwinning can sustain strain hardening and suppress plastic instability.
The combined operation of dislocation glide and deformation twinning can contribute to high ductility.
The quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy will have a higher strain-hardening rate than its quaternary and ternary subsets under identical room-temperature tensile testing.
The quinary alloy will have greater tensile ductility than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
The quinary alloy will develop a higher deformation-twin or nanotwin density than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
Yield-strength differences between the quinary alloy and its subsets will be modest.
The predicted mechanical-property differences will correlate with lower measured stacking-fault energy and increased twin density in the quinary alloy.
Changing the testing temperature can alter the strength, ductility, and deformation response.
Differences in processing or phase purity may alter the proposed comparison.
Failure to observe lower stacking-fault energy, increased twinning, or a correlation of these variables with enhanced strain hardening and ductility would falsify the proposed mechanism.
